voice_event.text: The crucified one, and the one we met in the poor. When the devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple with a crown of gold, the saint kept silence a long time, then said he would not believe Christ had come unless he came showing the marks of his wounds. That is the Lord we knew. And at a city gate a soldier cut his one cloak in two for a naked beggar whom everyone passed; that night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What his death meant to us we kept at the hours. At the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, and took away the debt that could not be paid. The good news as we told it: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation.

confidence.divergence_note: Genuinely shared - all three founding voices, both nodes: Martin sees him, Cassian's elders discern him, Vincent hears him quote Scripture. The visibility of the enemy is Sulpitius's emphasis, and the historicity of the northern appearances is not assessed here (carried by virtus / power's Reported-Experience Status). No Latin lemma sought - common vocabulary; daemonio meridiano is Gibson's editorial Latin at Inst. X.1.

Documented as to existence, office, and reputation: Sulpitius's Life, Letters, Dialogues, and Sacred History within or just after Martin's own lifetime, corroborated independently by Gennadius ch. XIX (ancient text: "monk and bishop," "a man famous for signs and wonders and virtues"). Everything narrated of him rests on one author, so every story is Widely Accepted, never Documented, at the narrative level (Doc_01 §2.2's rule that one ancient witness is not multiple independent sources); the two stories whose narrative claim is the wonder itself are Tier 3. The year of his birth, of the cloak, of the discharge, and of the election are not given in the text (the emperor is "Julian Caesar," the monastery's founding "after 371" only in the editorial introduction). His death in 397 is the horizon's own fixed point. Whether Sulpitius's virtus-organized Life is modelled on the Vita Antonii (Stancliffe, row 18, unread) is open and bears on how much of G6 is the north's own literary form, not on any fact about Martin.

The wording is Documented as Sulpitius's own text (Vita ch. XXIV, read at its locus for this record). The event is a Tier-3-shaped wonder - the devil appearing as Christ in Martin's cell - told by an author who was not present and who says he had it "from the lips of Martin himself"; Roberts's endnote 40 at the same locus records the editor's own doubt about the narrative. What this record carries as load-bearing is the formation ideal the words state (the Christ this world would own is the one who suffered), not the event; the words are Martin's as the tradition of Tours attributed them to him, never independently corroborated.

voice_event.text: He went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is what we were taught at the sixth hour of prayer - the spotless Sacrifice offered up to the Father. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. At the ninth hour he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. And the difference it made for us was this: a man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's.

glosses.translational_sense: Not a short waiting period before a near-default infant baptism: at Tours the state could last years into adult soldiering, and it is where our literature locates the first breaking-through of Martin's power.
false_friend: a brief administrative waiting period before an expected infant baptism

results.message: What does purity of heart mean?

voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text: A heart cleared to charity. Among the brethren at Marseilles it was the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, short of the kingdom itself - the definite mark at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation was aimed. By it all of these were ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, taught it this way: every art has some goal and some end of its own, and so does the monk's profession. Its end is the kingdom of God; its immediate goal is purity of heart, without which no one can gain that end, to be aimed at as if on a definite mark, like an archer's target. So the whole southern formation program served that mark. Discretion was the virtue that kept every other virtue from destroying itself, the royal road between excess and slackness. The eight faults were the numbered combats fought in order. And the first lesson of all was laying every rising thought bare to the senior before any deed, because a thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil.

glosses.plain_meaning: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."
glosses.quick_meaning: The act that makes a monk - a death to the world of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest stage. And the Church still fetches renunciants for its sees.
glosses.translational_sense: 'So renunciation means giving everything up - poverty, celibacy, leaving society for good?' - that is only the first and easiest of three stages for us, "of what is not our own"; the real renunciation is of what belongs to us, our affections and our will, a death "to this world" that extends what every baptized Christian renounced at the font - and after which the Church still comes to fetch the renunciant to be its bishop.
false_friend: giving things up - poverty, celibacy, "detachment" - as the whole of the monastic act
a heroic once-for-all rejection of society
self-denial for its own sake

glosses.plain_meaning: For us perfection is the summit of a graded ascent, not a state of being without fault. It is the declared subject of the Institutes, "the attainment of the perfect life." It is reached "not ... simply by self-denial ... unless there is that charity," climbed "from this fear to hope, from hope to the love of God." And at the summit we confess it is a thing "we cannot even make the effort to obtain ... without the mercy and inspiration of God."
glosses.quick_meaning: The summit of a graded ascent - fear, then hope, then love - with charity as its substance. Not flawlessness, and never reached without grace.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Perfection - do you mean sinlessness, an impossible standard?' - no: a graded ascent with charity as its substance and love at its top, measured by a goal rather than by faultlessness, whose stages are fear, hope and love, and whose summit is the confession that neither the effort nor the understanding of the effort is one's own; at Tours, simply a word of praise.

glosses.plain_meaning: In Cassian's Marseilles, discretion is the virtue by which every other is kept from destroying itself. It is "the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator," the "eye and light of the body," the "royal road" between excess and slackness. It is gained "only ... by true humility." glosses.quick_meaning: The virtue that keeps every other virtue from ruining itself. The royal road between excess and slackness, gained only by showing one's thoughts to the elders.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Discretion - you mean tact, or knowing when to keep quiet?' - no: the regulator of all the virtues, awarded that title by a council of Egyptian fathers, whose whole substance is the elders' judgment received through humility and disclosure, a money-changer's test of every thought on a royal road where "extremes meet" - a gift of grace, not a temperament.
false_friend: tact, prudence, or confidentiality
discernment as a private spiritual intuition or a decision-making technique
moderation as common sense

confidence.divergence_note: Cross-voice: the word and the act are shared across both nodes and a fourth voice (Salvian, who also uses it of the baptismal renunciation every Christian made at the font); the threefold schema is Cassian's alone and framed as Paphnutius's Egyptian teaching. Tours has the thing counselled and done without the technical term. Pruned from Doc_03's Tier-1 estimate because it does not organize independently of the pattern in which the renunciant returns to the Church as a bishop.

Weighted to Cassian: the technical sense is his and received (Moses, Paphnutius, Chaeremon, Nesteros); Sulpitius uses the word only as ordinary praise, and there is no doctrine of perfection at Tours in what was read. Two coverage limits bear on this term and are not filled: Conf. XXIII ("sinlessness") is unread and Conf. XII "On Chastity" is excised. The Latin perfectio is not attested in the vendored translation.

Documented as an author, a corpus, and a founder: the Institutes (for Castor, before the Conferences), the Conferences in three parts to named Gallic dedicatees (Part II not later than 426 on the vendored edition's own reasoning from Honoratus's title), and Gennadius ch. LXII (ancient text) on the two houses at Marseilles, "one for men and one for women, which are still standing." Contested [CT] is what his Thirteenth Conference meant in relation to Augustine and whether "semi-Pelagian" is fair (Chadwick vs. Casiday, Doc_01 §7) - carried at gallic.term.grace and gallic.term.free-will, not resolved here. The interval between his Egyptian journey and his writing in Gaul is not stated in this world's own documents and is not computed. Three of his texts are absent from the vendored English edition by the translator's own excision (Conf. XII, XXII; Inst. VI - row 11). He never mentions Martin, and no Native voice narrates his reaction to Prosper or Augustine - the controversy he is famous for has no narrative form in any Native voice (Doc_09 §8 item 5). Every locus below read directly at Doc_09.

The best-attested cross-node term in the lexicon: Sulpitius (Tours) and Cassian (Marseilles) use it independently, and Gennadius and Salvian corroborate. Vincent of Lerins never uses it of himself in what was read; that absence is stated, not filled. The three-kinds taxonomy (coenobite, anchorite, Sarabaite) is Cassian's alone and is framed by him as Egypt's own account, not Gaul's.

Both nodes, two voices: Sulpitius of individuals and oaths, Cassian of the whole way of life. The "goal and end" of the profession is Abbot Moses's teaching and received. The Latin professio is attested in the volume only in the editor's textual footnote to De Incarnatione, an unread work, and not in this sense.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text: Because the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, taught that the goal precedes the virtues. Every art has some goal and some end, and the monk's profession has the kingdom as its end and purity of heart as its immediate goal, without which no one can reach that end. That goal is what ranks everything else. Every fast, vigil, reading, renunciation, and manual labour is judged by whether it clears the heart for charity - an aid to perfection, never perfection itself. We believed it because it was handed down, not invented. The twelve psalms at the hours came from an angel; the goal itself came from the fathers. And we believed it because we saw what happens when a monk loses the mark. Two old men met after forty years - one said the sun never saw him eating, the other never angry. The one who kept the goal cleared his heart; the one who kept only the fast proved only endurance. So we aimed at the definite mark, the way an archer does.

confidence.divergence_note: Widely Accepted for the tradition and its transmission - Cassian's Institutes, written for Castor's new monastery in Gaul before the Conferences, present this as what "the venerable fathers" of Egypt received and handed on, and the office built on it is Documented as the southern node's own practice (Doc_05 §3). Contested for the specific attribution: the angel's appearance is the tradition's own claim about its origin, treated as the tradition treats it and not assessed for historicity. Cassian does not claim to have seen it or heard it from a named witness; he refers the reader to "ecclesiastical history." Origin disclosed in the narrative itself: this is Egypt's story, received at Marseilles, never a Gallic invention (Doc_06 §4(a)). Gibson's footnotes - the Eusebius/Sozomen cross-reference, the Benedictine Rule's Alleluia, the Second Council of Tours - are editorial (row 17) and are not the story's source. Every quoted phrase read at npnf211 divs iv.iii.ii.v-vi at Doc_09 construction; Registry row 7's own "daily-life" scope is applied here by a disclosed judgment call (Doc_09 §5).
